title: How startups beat incumbents: attack where big companies cannot or will not defend
summary: Jason Cohen argues that every big-company advantage (scale, brand, process, profit centers) creates a weakness a startup can exploit. He lists ten attack vectors: unquantifiable risks, niches below the materiality threshold, non-scalable work, founder-led support, new tech, drastic change, personality, non-zero-sum channels, being worse-but-acceptable, and low-cost against a profit center.

principles.text: A startup wins by doing what incumbents cannot or will not do; never fight them head-on where they are strong.
principles.quote: The way a startup wins, is to do things that incumbents cannot or will not do.

principles.text: Pick big bets by potential outcome, not ROI; incumbents avoid risks they can't quantify, so projects that look low-ROI face no competition.
principles.quote: A startup who selects "apparently" low-ROI projects, will probably have no competition from incumbents.

principles.text: Target niches too small for an incumbent's materiality threshold; the bigger the incumbent, the less competition you face.
principles.quote: The startup can focus on a niche and ICP that a big company cannot afford to target, either because that niche wouldn't hit the overall revenue materiality threshold, or wouldn't hit the one-team P&L threshold.

principles.text: Founders handling support personally gives an advantage incumbents can't match: product insight, retention, loyalty, forgiveness and word of mouth.
principles.quote: Some startups aren't interested in providing great support, but those that do are naturally and even effortlessly orders of magnitude better than a large incumbent.

principles.text: Do things that are hard to scale from day one; incumbents won't wait years to reach material revenue, but a slow ramp suits a startup.
principles.quote: if the product is naturally difficult to scale from day one, that's ideal for a startup.

principles.text: Most customers don't care about most dimensions; choose one or two to excel at, be worse-but-acceptable elsewhere, and win on price while incumbents chase complexity.
principles.quote: Most customers don't care about most things. This is great news for startups, who can select one or two dimensions to care about
